ingredients.item: fresh doraji , or 150 g dried, soaked 3 hours
A few drops of rice vinegar , optional

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: Blanch the cured, squeezed ribbons 3–4 minutes in unsalted boiling water — they should turn from opaque white to translucent-edged, still crunchy.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: a test ribbon bends into a U without breaking and keeps an audible crunch at the tooth. Overcooked doraji loses the crunch that is its whole identity; pull it while it still seems slightly too firm.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Cold rinse, drain, squeeze once more (gently this time — it has given enough), and cut into shorter lengths if it came in ribbons longer than 8 cm.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the ribbons are dry to the touch and springy.

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: The seasoning bowl: gochugaru, fish sauce, garlic, sugar, sesame oil worked to a paste; the warm-not-hot ribbons tossed through with the full-minute hand massage the namul family demands (#B16's law), scallions and sesame last.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the eating test: crunch first, the mild-bitter vegetal note under it, the dressing's savory-heat arriving second, and the slight bitterness lingering as the finish — that finish is doraji's signature, the reason it has kept its seat at the table beside sweeter vegetables that try harder to please.

storageNotes: Keeps 2–3 days refrigerated; the dressed ribbons hold crunch better than the blanched ones alone. Dried doraji, unsoaked, keeps a year in the pantry.

Variations: milder (half the gochugaru) as bibimbap's white vegetable; mixed with cucumber matchsticks for a summer crunch bowl; the blanched ribbons simply dressed with sesame oil and salt — the subtle fork the connoisseurs order.
